evidence: Quint. 1 pr. 21: liber prīmus ea quae sunt ante officium rhētoris continēbit
terms.comment: Of a whole that has the part in it: a book, a meal, a price. In the passive with the ablative, the part “is included in” it (Lewis & Short). “Including” is usually etiam or cum: omnēs, etiam līberī.

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.57: omnēs omnium cāritātēs patria ūna complexa est
terms.comment: Of something that takes in many things at once.

terms.gloss: put in, include (in a book, a letter)
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.19.3: nēminem inclūdere in dialogōs
Cic. Att. 1.16.10: ōrātiōnem in epistulam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its first sense is “shut in”: one includes something in a text, not a friend in a game.

terms.gloss: count among, include in a group
terms.grammar: phrase: numerus in the ablative, with a genitive
evidence: Cic. N. D. 3.48: in deōrum numerō habērī (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Phil. 2.33: mē adscrībe tālem in numerum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Cicero’s mē adscrībe tālem in numerum is “count me in that number”.

phrases.latin: Cārī sunt parentēs, cārī līberī, propinquī, familiārēs, sed omnēs omnium cāritātēs patria ūna complexa est
phrases.english: Dear are our parents, dear our children, our relatives and friends; but our country alone includes all our love for all of them

phrases.latin: nam liber prīmus ea quae sunt ante officium rhētoris continēbit
phrases.english: for the first book will include what comes before the teacher of rhetoric takes over

phrases.latin: sīc enim cōnstitueram, nēminem inclūdere in dialogōs eōrum quī vīverent
phrases.english: for I had decided to include in my dialogues no one who was still alive
